utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest last night.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It became chilly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I'm managing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just one or two more questions just in general, sort of background questions, before we turn to a bit more of your report itself. We left off at the end of the day talking about the statement that ethnic nationalism had become the only real value by mid-1992, which was leading me to this point when we ended yesterday: You also say in your report on page 28 that these things you've told us about practically meant -- I'm quoting now "practically meant that one's own --" that is, the phrase of concept of one's own, one's own people -- "had to be backed up even when they were evidently doing wrong." I was wondering if you could provide some additional insight to the Judges about what you meant about that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As usual your extraction of a sentence or even part of a sentence from the idea -- from the context in which it appears brings into question its meaning. If we look at the sentence as a whole, because I have it in the Croatian original -- I'd like to read it and then it will be quite clear what this is about. So it says: "The mechanisms of such national rationalisation is -- it is not difficult to understand the mechanisms of the social operation. Any potential authority dependent on the loyalty of the members of its own community, which practically meant that one's "own," that is, those who belong to my group had to be backed up even when they were evidently doing wrong because it meant fulfilling the basic task, the protection of one's "own," that is, a person who is in any post presuming authority, in this place, in that situation that person is there only because he or she belongs to a group. If he or she belongs to a group, then he/she must also stand behind it as a whole. Otherwise, that person loses the authority he enjoys with that group. Your Honours, may I continue, only two more sentences. Fortunately last night I went through my text once again and I was very grateful to you for taking out several sentences out of their context because it made me read the text with new eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me submit to you -- I'm not going to argue with you, but I have -- everyone in the courtroom has your report, and I believe that I have accurately pointed out certain passages to you which you've had every opportunity to explain and in many instances indeed have gone on at some length and have put any greater context on your statements as you wish. So I think you'll find, sir, that you've been afforded every opportunity to explain your report, which is the reason for my questions. Now, right above the passage you read to us just now, you say "The world was now divided nearly exclusively into 'us' and 'them' and the only line of distinction was that of the logic of national affiliation." Now, taking that also context of your report and the statement that you just told us about, can you give to the Judges some examples of where members of one group did something to back up that group even though it was a situation where that group had "evidently done wrong"? Can you give us some concrete examples of that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concrete examples for this claim -- actually, I mean history of the whole war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Countless cases in which an individual did -- committed acts which under normal circumstances -- for which under normal circumstances he would be brought to account, in such circumstances in which there is neither state, nor agencies of state power, in which everything is extemporised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, can you give me one specific example, sir. So far you haven't given us any specifics to back up your statement. Can you give me an example, please, of something that a senior Bosnian Croat official did to support his own group or one's own, as you say, even though that group had evidently done wrong. Can you give the Judges one example of that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One example of such behaviour -- one example of such behaviour is the conflict which arose regarding the distribution of fuel at a petrol pump in Novi Travnik. People who had words about the distribution of fuel on both sides were not brought to account by either commanding side. I think that there is a whole series of such examples, and I even quoted some of them, explaining that it is such situations which could arise to the atmosphere of mutual distrust.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving on to your report. Did the inhabitants of the medieval states such as Bosnia, Raska, and Hum, around the Mostar region, for example, did these people during medieval times have any notion of being Serbs or Croats or anything else?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those people, or to be quite precise, a segment of the population, that which belonged to the ruling elite, those people were aware of their membership in an ethnic community. Documents, unfortunately very few, from Hum, which you have just mentioned, demonstrate that there is an awareness of one's membership in an ethnic community, that there is awareness about the membership in a broader ethnic community, a kingdom. At lower social echelons, the majority of the population today, it is very difficult to say what they could really think, because the life of an overwhelming majority of them was not recorded in any written document at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say, then, sir, that among the -- perhaps the political or economic elites there might have been some sense of ethnic identification, but among the vast majority of, if we can use the term, "everyday people," there was not such ethnic identification?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was quite precise, because I also expressed the reservation as to how far our cognition can go, what is the scope of our cognition. In my field of work guesses can go only as far as reasonable doubt goes. Anything that is beyond that is not considered as knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, in that regard, sir, in fact do you have any way of proving who are what some might call the real descendants or the authentic descendants of the medieval Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I need to correct you and warn you that the medieval term for those people was Bosnjanin, that it was added that today it is to all intensive purpose impossible to show who is whose heir. Political upheavals have brought about immense ethnic and geographical changes so that today any attempt to establish who is whose direct descendant is practically tantamount to an illusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So can we understand from that, sir, that anyone who would attempt to say that any particular modern ethnic group are the most ancient people, if you will, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether that be claimed to be the Serbs or the Bosniaks or the Croats or, for that matter, somebody else. Nobody can really make that claim. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you use the word -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we can establish today with certainty is the moment when for the first time the documents mention members of those communities which we know today under their national names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your report, sir, you repeatedly used the word "cult," or at least that's the way it's translated in the English version. And just so there's no misunderstanding that we're not talking about something -- sometimes "cult" can have a particular other -- a number of meanings, I suppose. You're talking about religious groups here, in the sense of Catholic, Orthodox, Jews, or Muslims, for example. When you say "cult," you're talking about religious groups; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've give one story of a conflict in 1737 in Fojnica, page 11 of your report at the bottom. You say, "this speaks volumes about deep distrust and fear, which surfaced easily and caused violent behaviour." How is it that you draw such a broad conclusion from a particular anecdote from 1737?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident I described is an illustration of a fundamental idea. If, however, you want to have a list of all other similar events that are -- that we know about, then I could -- then I would have to present to that Honourable Court tomes and tomes of books. It is a historian's job to investigate events, and from those events to glean what -- those things which represent a pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if Bosnia's interreligious or inter-ethnic relations in the 19 -- sorry, let me start again. Given what you've told us about medieval history and leading up to the present time, is it your position that the inter-ethnic or interreligious relationships in Bosnia-Herzegovina or the former Yugoslavia, for that matter, in the 1960s, 1970s, 1980s were better or worse than the rest of Europe during the same period?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rest of Europe in this regard offers us a motley picture. If you want me to, we can draw a comparison with the situation in Belgium in the 1960s, the situation in Northern Ireland in the 1970s -- and in the 1970s and in the 1980s, but we can also draw comparison with the situation in Denmark and then all these pictures will prove to be very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, if relations were so bad and so -- just barely beneath the surface, going back to medieval times, as you seem to suggest, why then during the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s were there not a string of continuous conflicts? Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question, to begin with, contains something which is glaringly inaccurate. Between 1969 and 1971, there was an open conflict in the former Yugoslavia based precisely on ethnic sentiments. That conflict ended in a very crude repressive measure supplied by the State, and therefore it is not correct to say that there were no conflicts. Another thing: Such measures of extreme repression beyond any doubt instilled fear in people and prevented any public debate about those topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: While we're on this time period, sir, maybe could you just refresh both my memory and perhaps assist the Judges. There's been -- there's general knowledge of something that might be referred to as to "Croatian spring." When was that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is exactly what I referred to a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I just wanted to be sure if we were talk -- thinking the same thing or not. Now, you say that you left Sarajevo in 1993. Can you tell us how it is you left Sarajevo at that time under siege? How did you leave the city and why did you leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- in the war I was, among other things, the editor of a newspaper published -- which came into being in 1990, and the name of which was "Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the nature of that newspaper? What kind of -- what news or events or what have you, what did you cover? What was the paper about? What were the articles about?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a weekly which carried articles similar to the ones published by a news magazine. The fact that I was its editor and I became the editor when the previous editor left Sarajevo, enabled me to obtain the United Nations credentials. With these credentials I had the right to be transported by airplane, and that is how I was able to leave Sarajevo, in which no civilised life was possible at the time. So that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where did name of the newspaper "Herceg-Bosna" come from?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name comes from the Croatian tradition in which, since the nineteenth century, the name used for Bosnia and Herzegovina has also been Herceg-Bosna. One needs to understand what I bring in my expert report, and that is that the term "Bosnia and Herzegovina" became a political and a geographical term only in 1878. It appeared for the first time in German, in the German language, written as "Bosnien und Herzegowina." Before that, that term was not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say you received UN credential, can you tell us a bit more about what that means. I'm not sure what you mean when you say you received UN credentials.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm not clear why this expert is being asked about facts. I don't see the point. I really don't see the point of that. Why would this Honourable Court want to know why he obtained credentials or why he didn't obtain credentials. Is that what he is here for? We know exactly what this witness is here for and what answers he is supposed to give, so I don't know why we should all know why he obtained the UN credentials, for what reasons, and I would kindly ask my learned friend to stick to the topic for which this witness has been called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, whenever we have an expert witness, Mr. Krsnik, I think you're entitled in your direct examination first to establish this expert witness; second, ask some questions about his report, that is, his statement. During the cross-examination, of course the Prosecutor is entitled to ask any questions which arises from the report itself, but also the Prosecutor is entitled to ask any questions about the background of this expert witness, to challenge the credibility of that witness. I don't think anything is wrong with asking this question to that witness. And this witness has already answered that question. I think he's entirely in the line of our proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I agree with everything that you have just said, if only this was adhered to. I just want to avoid the situation that we saw -- I believe that it was at the detriment of the Defence that we saw with the first expert witness who was here and who in the cross-examination, just like you said, it did not end in this way. Here I mean the expert on demography that we had here who testified and who came here to testify about demographics, and in the cross-examination you -- I believe you remember the whole situation, that something was introduced that didn't have anything to do with the expert witness, with his testimony, or with the topic for which he was called. The testimony all focussed on the book that he said he didn't know anything about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'll take note of your statement just now and I'll look into the transcript about that first expert witness. But now I think you have to allow us to continue. Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you raise in your answer the reason that you were able to leave Sarajevo during these circumstances, that you obtained something which you called a UN credential. And I just don't know what you mean by that. What papers did you receive from the UN, you say, that allowed you to leave Sarajevo at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not even a paper. It was a plastic ID badge or card which showed that the person holding it was a journalist, that he was on a United Nations list as a journalist, and that he was entitled to use the services of the UN agencies, amongst which was the entitlement to use the United Nations aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you at any time during the early to mid-1990s have any role in, any position, function, membership in the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Never in my whole life have I been a member of any political organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during that same time period did you have any role or relationship with either the HV or the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay in Sarajevo, from mid-1992, I had a military ID of the HVO issued in Sarajevo. I would like to add to that that already from mid-1992 in Sarajevo there was not a single man of my age, and I was 35/36 at the time, who didn't carry a military ID. Due to a chronic illness, I did not have to do the compulsory military service in the former Yugoslavia. I was given a certificate that I'm not capable of serving in the army. Therefore, my military ID served as some sort of protection in the conditions of the lack of public order that prevailed in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say that you -- in the CV that was provided to us, sir, by counsel, you talk about being employed at the history institute. And I'm not sure. Is that the same place you're working today, or have you changed jobs since 1993 -- or 1997? It wasn't clear to me, sir. Where are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I was quite clear and precise and that my CV is very precise in those terms. From 1997 [As interpreted] until 1993 I worked at the history institute in Sarajevo. From 1993 I have worked at the institute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is a mistake in the transcript which I would like to correct. Can you please look at the transcript. It is not 1997 but 1987. That is what the gentleman said. He worked between 1987 and 1993 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question specifically, sir, is: Where are you employed at the present time? Please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Institute of the Croatian Academy of Arts and Sciences in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that a private institution or is that a institution of the state of the Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an institution that belongs to the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts. And the whole academy and therefore the institute itself are funded from the state budget. And in such a small state as Croatia, which on top of it is also very poor, it is inconceivable to -- for anybody to engage in the kind of work that I'm doing if this was not funded from the state budget. There is no other source of financing that could provide for this kind of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In what capacity, sir, are you testifying here in The Hague? Are you testifying here as a private individual, or are you testifying here on behalf of the institute or on behalf of the Croatian government, or in what capacity exactly are you here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, from now on I will disallow such questions, and I would kindly ask you to accept my view. I believe that Mr. Scott has gone over the top and he is here because the Defence has called him, and what Mr. Scott is now doing is very typical of his cross-examinations. So far please disallow any further questions of this kind. I strongly object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, we understand where you are going in this question, but we all know that this witness came here as the expert witness called by the Defence counsel. You may put your question in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You talked about the institute, sir, being state-funded. Is the report that you've given to the Judges which is marked as D1/316, was your report and the work on that report state-funded?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you receive any payment or compensation, remuneration of any sort for the work you did in preparing this document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent my invoice to counsel Krsnik, based on the customs applied to the work of experts engaged by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when did you write or prepare this report, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prepared my report towards the end of 2001 and the beginning of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of your report, did you consider or rely upon any significant volume of material, source material or information, which is not described or cited in your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For my report, I used a vast amount of sources of various nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is all that material reflected in your report, in your footnotes -- what I'm trying to understand, sir, have you given us all the information you've relied -- substantially relied upon? Not -- I allow certainly there may be other things that came to mind. But generally sir, can the Judges understand that the authorities on which you base and your conclusions are those cited in this 29-page document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been a historian professionally for 20 years now. The vast amount of documents coming from various sources has created a base from which I derive the substance for my reports. As for the footnotes, they will reflect only the documents that I am referring to directly at a given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of preparing your report, sir, did you take instruction or direction from any person other than Mr. Krsnik and his colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that you also worked on the Defence team in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received an offer from the Defence team in that case to prepare a report. I indeed prepared that report, but it hasn't been used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it true that you also worked on the Kordic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My report has been admitted in the Kordic case. And if you read this report more carefully, you will notice that I am referring to what I did in the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the report that you've given to the Judges in this case, marked as D1/316, is that substantially the same report that you prepared in the Blaskic case and the same report that you prepared in the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These three reports can be regarded as one whole. What differentiates them, what is different, are the years in which I have matured as a historian, during which I have deepened my insight and during which I have been able to look at the things from a new perspective, from a new angle. And I hope that the day will come when all these reports will end up as parts of a book. However, this is not the job of this Honourable Court, isn't it [As interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question very concretely, sir: If I put before you the two prior reports and put it together with this one, are you telling these Judges that the three documents would look substantially different, or would they in fact be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would not be essentially the same because they are talking in different ways about the things which is the subject of the matter before this Honourable Court and in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But you did not testify, correct, in either the Blaskic case or the Kordic case? Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Blaskic case, I repeat, the Defence team did not use my services any further. My report wasn't used and my services were not used. The Defence team in the Kordic case submitted my report to the Tribunal, and I did not testify before the Trial Chamber. Why is that the case, you would have to ask the Defence team in the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, your real expertise and what you've studied and what you teach about is medieval history; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question, sir, again contains an inaccurate fact. The question of my real expertise is not the same that I teach. I consider myself, very immodestly, an expert on the issue of modern national identities in the area of the former Yugoslavia. My second professional specialty is the history of medieval times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of modern Yugoslav history, sir, your report seems to rely rather heavily on a man named Benedict Anderson and another man named Milorad Akmecic. Do you consider Mr. Akmecic a reliable source?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Akmecic, but Ekmecic, with an "E."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question stands, sir. Do you consider Mr. Ekmecic a reputable academic source?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider Mr. Ekmecic one of the better experts on the materials which lend themselves as the sources for the history of the area of the former Yugoslavia. If I may draw your attention to my report, you will notice that in it I have used Milorad Ekmecic's work mostly as my source for the facts. My attitude towards Milorad Ekmecic's authority and the authority of Benedict Anderson differs greatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say relied on Mr. Ekmecic for your facts, your report is primarily based on secondary sources, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report I have quoted only secondary sources. And for the research, which is another thing and differs from writing a report, I used a number of primary sources that were available to me. In all that I used my experience that I have gathered over the period of 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We've talked about Dr. Robert Donia. Are you actually familiar with Dr. Donia's CV? Have you ever actually seen his CV?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps we'll assist you then and assist the Chamber -- if the usher could assist in showing you Exhibit 943.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And usher, I'm going to suggest that the documents have been arranged in a single bundle in the order in which I hope to use them, so you could put the whole bundle in front of the witness, please. It would save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, had you indeed wanted to save time, you could have given it yesterday, rather than put up this whole performance with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I don't think Mr. Scott has decided to use it until now. It depends on your direct examination and the cross-examination. But you made a very good suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, counsel has had the entire bundle since yesterday. And we had not gotten to any exhibits with the witness this morning until now, and I don't see any reason to belabour the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you could look at Exhibit 943. I think you said yesterday you've never met Mr. Donia. Have you? Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've never spoken to him.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in terms of any of his writings as reflected, his books or articles, reviews, reflected on Exhibit P943, you've not reviewed any of his working papers or discussed with him at all the methodology that he applied; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to his writings, I read them carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, sir. The working papers, -- I assume when you prepare a book or a paper, apart from the final product you have a large set of working papers, notes, source material. You've not reviewed any of Dr. Donia's working papers and you don't know the methodology that he applied in preparing these books, articles, reviews; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said yesterday that Dr. Donia, because he was working, you say at Merrill Lynch at the time, was not reviewing the literature. He was not staying in touch with the literature on the former Yugoslavia. Now, how do you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because reading that literature is my livelihood. Because to be able to keep up with literature, I need eight working hours every day; sometimes even more than eight working hours a day. In my kind of work, there are no weekends, there are no Saturdays, there are no Sundays.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, how do you know that Dr. Donia wasn't reading Yugoslav literature every night and every weekend? The fact of the matter is you simply don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot affirm that I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, why --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is -- excuse me. May I finish. Your Honours, may I finish my sentence? But there is a highly reasonable doubt that a man who works for a major investment house and does it full time, of ten hours, who also has to commute to get to his workplace and from it, who has a family life, has such -- that he has such physical abilities that he can devote three or four hours a day to keep in touch, only in touch. Not follow the literature, but keep in touch with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, why would you come into this courtroom under oath and make the completely bald assertion that Dr. Donia was not reading the literature on the former Yugoslavia, would having any basis to say so?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that he does not read.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And obviously from his CV he obviously publishes quite extensively, does he not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall we look at the dates of the things that he published?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, why do you think that you as an academic in medieval history are more qualified than Dr. Donia to express views on what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I am not an expert on the medieval history. I do not think -- I do not consider myself better qualified than Dr. Donia. I merely warned -- I merely drew attention to some facts related to Dr. Donia which in the same way that you are applying to bring into question my credibility attests to the credibility of Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. -- If Dr. Donia, sir, is not to be trusted as a source, why is it that indeed you cite him as a source in a number of places in your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said it very precisely, that when reading Dr. Donia's texts I saw two faces of a historian, and I drew the attention to the fact to -- in his book "Islam under the Double Eagle," I think it is a very valuable and interesting book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you worked -- ever worked or been involved with any group of association which might be called or considered a human rights group?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall being involved in a publication called "The Ethnic Cleansing of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina 1991-1993," in which you are thanked for your contribution on the last page along with people like Marko Rados, Ivan Bagaric, Jozo Maric, and a number of others? What contribution did you make to that publication?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if he is talking about a publication, about a document, then shouldn't the witness be shown it rather than ask him to speak off the top of his head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'd like to see what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You don't recall it, sir? Before I do that, you don't recall being involved in a publication by that name?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance. I only brought one copy because I didn't realise that the witness would draw this into question, and it's not marked. But perhaps the usher can give us an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we are once again in a disagreeable situation. The Defence cannot even get the text of it to cast a look at it. I don't know if it is translated. I don't know what we can -- with this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I ask to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, furnish us with more information, background information about this article, this publication, whatever, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Has it been translated, you know, when it was published, you know, where did you find it, or something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, it appears to be a publication titled "Ethnic Cleansing of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina 1991-1993," published in Mostar in August 1993, with an introduction by Mate Boban dated the 25th of August, 1993. Printed by the -- printed in Grude. The publisher being the Office of the President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And it's not -- at least the one that I have with me -- obviously the original document -- well, presumably the original document, given the information I've just given you, is written in Croatian. I don't have it with me, and frankly I'm surprised that it would be an issue. I expected the witness would identify his involvement in this. I'm happy to make extra copies of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you are allowed to show this document to the witness. And be sure to furnish with us a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Exhibit number is P960.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could finish on this point, then, I think by that time we'd be ready for the break then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can answer straight away. When the Prosecutor described what it was about, I then remembered that there was indeed such a publication in which I do not figure as an author of any kind. And for your information, that publication exists even in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. We have it in front of us as P960.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You didn't think, sir, that in giving us the CV that in your in your CV it was worth telling the Judges about your involvement with that publication?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Scott, you know, the witness is -- did not answer your previous question, that is, what contribution did you make to that publication. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the gentleman, the witness, has been answering for the past five minutes that he does -- he did not figure here as an author and that he had nothing to do with this publication. I really don't know how to interpret all this. He has answered immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we have that, you know, article at our hands, you know, but the witness said -- the article said that the witness was thanked for his contribution to that article, so the Prosecution asked him a question, "What kind of contribution did you make to that article?", which is a very logical question. We are waiting for the answer from this witness. Witness, you may answer that question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is my contribution to that publication? That is something that one should ask its authors. My name appears here alongside 30 or so other names. I really know one of the authors of this publication. But what Ms. Vesna Ivanovic saw as my contribution, that is something that you should ask her.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You really don't know, sir? You really -- you're telling these three Judges under oath that you don't know what you were being thanked for?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- the last question, I believe, before the break: Can you tell us, sir, have you written or assisted or contributed to any publications about war crimes allegedly committed by Bosnian Croats against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We can stop there, Mr. President, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in your paper, I believe it may have been mentioned yesterday, but I'm not -- I admit I'm not completely sure. But I -- the phrase "internal secession" has been used. I think you said that some other historian had coined the phrase. But what do you understand that phrase to mean, "internal secession"?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't the one who coined it. I found it in a text. I shall repeat it once again -- of a professor of political sciences teaching at the Central European University in Budapest, Daniele Conversini. The term "internal secession" according to his interpretation, means separation of the parts of the former Yugoslavia and unification with Serbia and Montenegro. And the whole process looks as if Slovenia and then Croatia were the first to try to secede from Yugoslavia. To -- in confirmation of Conversini's conclusion, in the text I quoted also a diary note of the then-member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia from Serbia, Borislav Jovic, which -- of course if it is to be believed directly, confirms -- directly confirms Conversini's conclusion. I do not know if Conversini was aware of that material, but if he -- even if he did, he did not quote it or directly use it, and so it seemed to me that it might be useful to draw the attention to this confirmation of the thesis propounded by my distinguished colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, apart from discussing medieval history, sir, two main points of your report appear to be that the Serbs started the war and the Serbs in the various conduct that they were engaged in were worse in that respect than the Croats and Muslims. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And taking -- assuming that your observations in that respect are true, assuming that the Serbs started it and assuming that the Serbs were worse than the other two principal parties, do you see that as somehow being helpful to Mr. Naletilic's defence or somehow contrary to what you understand to be the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that I follow your question with difficulty, because after all I am not all that familiar with the entirety of your induction -- indictment and especially not with the -- I'm not that familiar with the strategy and all the postulates of the Defence. In my work, I was guided chiefly by what I might call my professional consciousness, my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm just trying -- let me put it different, then. Assuming again that your two observations are true. And I'm not quarreling with them at the moment. Does the fact that the Serbs did it first, or did it on a larger scale, reduce the seriousness of Croat or Bosniak crimes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The seriousness of any crime cannot be reduced. The question remains about the context within which every individual crime took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your report, when you called -- when you talk about the Bosniak Army, you describe it as, in quotation marks, "BH Army." Why do you say BH Army in quotation marks?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The quotation marks are due to the fact that, in contrast with the other two armies, which resorted to national names in the identification, the Muslim -- the Bosniak Army used a name which did not imply that it was ethnically exclusive, as the case was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On page 16 of your report, you used the phrase "anti-democratic nationalism." Can you tell us what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just tell me what the context is, because the pages in English and Croatian do not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, if it will assist you, if you can find your footnote 41, the use of the term -- use of that term falls between footnote 41 and footnote 42 of your text. We've talked about nationalism, sir, but you specifically use or have quoted from somewhere, you have quotes "anti-democratic nationalism." And what is anti-democratic nationalism, as opposed to just plain old nationalism?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a term which I took over from a Hungarian historian Istvan Bibo. He uses a whole string of terms which I quoted here. The "insecurity of national frameworks," "existential fear for the community," "anti-democratic nationalism." In other words, these terms are used to describe a type of political culture, which in Istvan Bibo's view, exists in central -- which existed in Central East Europe in the mid-twentieth century.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, I must admit, sir, that I have your answer, and I think I understand the words you've used, but I still don't know what is meant by the concept of "anti-democratic nationalism." You've given us the source and you've talked about Mr. Bibo, but what specifically does "anti-democratic nationalism" mean?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to Mr. Bibo, there is a possibility for nationalism to be democratic, and he sees such a type of nationalism in the majority of the Western European countries. And as for the world that he lives in, he believes that the nationalism there doesn't have that characteristic; in other words, that it is anti-democratic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, moving on -- and perhaps some of these things will come up again -- page 17 -- excuse me, on page 17 of your report, you say -- and it's right after footnote 47, if that will assist you. About the middle of the page of the English version on page 17, you said, "For the Croats, this same 'Yugoslavia' quickly became a kind of prison. This should definitely be brought into connection with the centralist political organisation of the country and the privileged position occupied in it by the Serbs." Now, what are you saying here, sir, when you say that for Croats Yugoslavia became a kind of prison? How so?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am quoting one of the largest authorities for that issue, today the respectable historian Ivo Banac, and his key work for this area, for this historical area, and I'm talking about the picture of Yugoslavia in the minds of those who consider themselves Croats. They consider to be deprived of equal opportunities in the society. And if you don't enjoy equal opportunities in a society, then that society is for you and in your perception a sort of a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Might the -- sir, might the Bosnians, the Muslims, in the territory claimed by Herceg-Bosna considered Herceg-Bosna to be a prison for them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably just in the way Croats felt like being in some sort of a prison in the areas controlled by the government in Sarajevo and by the BH Army. And as Croats and Muslims certainly felt this like some sort of a prison in the areas controlled by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So would that --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Sorry. I thought you were finished. So with that explanation, sir, the answer to my question is yes, you can conceive or would agree that many of the Muslims in the territory claimed by Herceg-Bosna may have felt that Herceg-Bosna for them was a prison; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer directly yes or no, but if we apply the principles of the strict ethnic affiliation, they may have felt that way indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On that same page, sir, you use the term "mass political mobilisation." It appeared between your footnote 46 and footnote 47. And at least as applied to what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, what do you mean by "mass political mobilisation"?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mass political mobilisation is form of political activity typical of modern societies. In that form of political activity, in a dynamic relationship between the political elite and masses, there is an area of political activity. The political elite listens to the requests and the opinions of the masses, indirectly influences those opinions and uses those masses at the same time in order to achieve some of their political goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give the Judges, please, just one or two concrete examples of form of mass political mobilisation. How was it in Bosnia-Herzegovina that the masses were mobilised, politically mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An example of political mass mobilisation is the notorious murder of the participants in a wedding in the old part of Sarajevo which took place in March 1992. It was a wedding of two Serbs who came to an Orthodox church to -- in Sarajevo to be married. There was an incident in which one of the participants in the wedding, a Serb, lost his life. With the help of the mass media, a picture was created according to which the person -- it was not the person AA who killed the person BB but, rather, the whole entity called Muslims shot at the whole entity called the Serbs. It is a classical example how mass political mobilisation can be generated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How does mass political mobilisation relate to such things as the use of culture religion, art, or music?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cultural elements in this form of political activity become the marker of affiliation or belonging to a community. It is a sign showing to others that the person belongs to one community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that regard, sir, would it be fair to say - and just bear we me for a moment on this - would it be fair to say that nationalist fervour or identity can be fostered one way as by promoting or strengthening the group identity of your own group by means of common culture, common tradition, common heroes, and another way is to denigrate or make less legitimate in some fashion the other group? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a second way in which this can be done. You are right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And would it also be correct, sir, that some things can be done to increase the national fervour of one group, to strengthen perhaps the identity of that group, without explicitly attacking the other group; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The choice of such methods, if there indeed is a choice at all, will depend on the social context in which such things happen. In some social circumstances the answer is yes; in some others, on the other hand, the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of your historical work, sir, which you've told us since yesterday is quite broad, did you come across -- are you familiar with two individuals, one named Jure Francetic and the other one Rafael Boban?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges, please, who was Jure Francetic? And if it will assist you, I will draw you're attention and the Chamber's attention to -- it should be 830.2, which you should have -- it should be in the bundle in the order in which we've been proceeding. There's a Croatian language original or a copy of the original, sir, from a book called "Who is Who in the NDH." And to put the topic in context, can you tell the Judges who was the "NDH."

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NDH was a state creation formed after the German army, followed by the Italian army, occupied the former Yugoslavia. Under the patronage of Germany and Italy, in the territory of the former Kingdom of Yugoslavia, a number of different political and state creations were formed, one of them being also the NDH.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: NDH standing for what, sir? What's the full name?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during what time did the Independent State of Croatia exist?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 1941 and 1945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may ask what is -- what is the relevance of this with our case and with this expert witness's report and what is the relevance of Croatia during the Second World War to our case. You will remember that the Prosecutor has tried to have the same document tendered through another witness, but it wasn't admitted. If you will remember, you did not admit that document. Now it is marked as a new document, but it isn't because it now appeared for the second time in a bundle. The first time it appeared it was through another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, you may establish the relevance of your questions to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The relevance is, Your Honour -- and it ties directly into what this witness has testified to in the last two days -- the Chamber has allowed him to give the broadest possible testimony on a range of topics. He's talked about nationalism, the use of symbolism, the use of common heroes to create group identification. The Chamber has heard for the past one year about -- from many witnesses, including Defence witnesses, about a certain song called "Jure and Boban," that certain Muslims were forced to sing that was the anthem, the organisational anthem of the HVO. And this witness can tell us -- I think the Chamber after all this time might want to hear a little bit more about who this "Jure and Boban" was and what the song was. It's highly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then this is the way my learned friend could have put the question. But the song, the so-called "Jure and Boban" with which we wanted to assist the Chamber and even had it translated, you did not admit because you didn't consider it to be relevant. That is why I raised the issue of relevance. It says on the list that this document is not tendered. That's the last document on the Prosecution's list. We have even translated it. You haven't admitted it. We wanted to tender it in evidence. You didn't admit it, obviously, considering it not to be relevant. I really, really wonder about the relevance of all these issues, questions touching upon Croatia during the Second World War. Secondly, the Prosecutor cannot give testimony by claiming that this song, the folk song or whatever that song was, was the HVO hymn. This is not correct because the HVO anthem is public, has been published, and the Prosecutor can certainly gain access to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me you're talking about two matters. The first matter is admission of the documents. The other matter is the particular question the Prosecution is going to ask. Mr. Scott, you may ask this question. We believe that all the Judges would like to know about this historical person and the relevance of this person to the present case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to where we start add few moments ago, sir, with that -- some additional background in mind now. I asked you if you knew who the two individuals, one named Jure Francetic and the other one Rafael Boban, not to be confused with Mate Boban. If you knew who those two individuals were and you said yes. So let's start with Mr. Francetic? Who was he and what role did he play in World War II?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an officer of the army of the state, which was called the Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He's described here in this publication, sir, and it's not my word but the publication in Croatian language, he's described as an Ustasha general, correct, in Exhibit 830.2?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was an Ustasha officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact if we look at the original Croatian language excerpt of the publication, on page 118, do you see that he has a -- the letter "U" prominently displayed on the front of his helmet?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in a similar fact --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. If I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you can also clearly see that he is wearing a military uniform, so he is an army officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course. And can you in a similar fashion, sir, tell us what you know about Rafael Boban?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also an officer of the army of the state called the Independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again regarded as an Ustasha commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Weren't both Mr. Boban and Mr. Francetic notorious for being involved in very extreme activities during the war, not -- given the descriptions, won't say more except what's stated in Exhibit 830.2. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time the Prosecution, with the assistance of the transcript that was previously provided by the Defence, which has been marked as D1/233, which I think has been provided for the Chamber's assistance, I hope, in the bundle -- with that in hand, Mr. President, we would propose for the video booth to play Exhibit P945, which is a tape of the song "Jure and Boban" -- what we call "Jure and Boban."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, do we have the translation here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There's one in B/C/S -- excuse me, I'll say Croatian. And the first page of that exhibit should be in English. If you don't have it, I can certainly put it on the ELMO, but -- it follows immediately after Exhibit 830.2, I believe. Do you have it, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then I request the booth to please play Exhibit P945.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, moving on then. You've indicated, again in your report, that it's your view that the Serb group in the former Yugoslavia initiated the war, which became a war concerning territory, and carried out a number of notorious acts; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And isn't it true, sir, I put the Prosecution case to you, that as I said to you a few moments ago, perhaps not identically and perhaps not as extreme, but isn't it true, sir, that the HDZ and the HVO embarked on a similar programme in connection with the project, if we can use that term, called "Herceg-Bosna"?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thanked you earlier this morning because you made me reread my text and look at it in a new way and even draw conclusions that I couldn't draw when I was writing the text. My conclusion would be as follows: The political leaderships of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, probably under the pressure of the political leadership from Zagreb, by their activities, actually, preserved Bosnia and Herzegovina despite the pressure which came from beneath to unite those parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina in which Croats constituted a majority with the Republic of Croatia. In keeping with what I wrote in my report, one can clearly see that the mass political will led towards the redefining of the borders, whereas the political elite, by its actions and manipulations, managed to channel that request in such a way as to keep the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the symbolical level, what is formed is the thing that we call the view of the world. The political leadership at precisely that level managed to preserve the picture of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In every official document starting with IDs, which are called personal IDs, to driving licences and everything else that is perceived as icons in the life -- everyday life of every person, the picture of Bosnia and Herzegovina remained present. If you want me to, if you need it, I will gladly point to all the places from which you took parts of the sentences out of the context, and I will read the entire context surrounding these words, and then you will be able to draw the same conclusion as I did. The technique that you're using is not unusual. You are taking parts of a thought and then you put them together in a new way in order to prove your thesis. However, I don't think you have been successful in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that, sir. I appreciate your commentary. The report is in evidence. The entire report is in the chamber, and everyone can read the entire report and draw their own conclusions ultimately, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, after this tape I expected, I don't know, to see the purpose -- I guess the Prosecutor knows -- suffer the questions [As interpreted]. But I think it would be good manners to tell the Defence and this Honourable Court, I believe, which year is it? Who are these people? What is it? What does it represent? Who recorded it? When? Where? It could have been shot yesterday in my yard. I mean, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I thought we have already passed that issue already. So you want to go back to that issue again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I don't. It would be good manners. It would be civil to know some basic information, some basic things about this tape. But never mind, Your Honours. Forget it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe the Prosecutor will take your advice in his future proceedings. You may move on, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I just say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have sometimes said, Mr. Krsnik, maybe a little cruelly to the Prosecution that we're not children. Credit us with some intelligence. We don't need to have everything spelled out to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why, of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we move on, then, perhaps -- in light of the exchange in the last few minutes to comment only to this extent. The song was played for itself, not about anything else that was depicted or about what was happening or not happening, but for the Chamber to hear, I think for the first time, this actual song being played. Now, I have heard no objection that that is not the "Jure and Boban" song. I've heard no objection that the transcription provided from the Defence -- it was a Defence prescription, D1/277 was not accurate. So and so there appears to be no dispute in the courtroom that the music -- the song has been played and the lyrics that were provided to the Chamber were accurate. And that was the only purpose it was provided to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think that's a matter for the admission of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: At a later stage. You may move on, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it correct that as you've told us in your report and as we've talked about since yesterday, that in fact not all, of course, but many of the Bosnian Croats, those represented by the HDZ and the HVO identified themselves with the term used yesterday was "the mother national state," that they identified, to use your terms, linked the future not to Bosnia-Herzegovina but to their mother country. As a step in that direction established Herceg-Bosna, the ultimate goal or hope of becoming part of Croatia. Isn't that what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure that your claim is accurate. How individuals perceived the establishment of Herceg-Bosna is very difficult to assess today what we know. Yes. The fact that there is only one problematic document of Herceg-Bosna and it explicitly says that it is a provisional product pending the resolution of the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What individuals expected in 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994 could be the subject of a very lengthy argument. It is also a fact that in view of the historical experience one could really expect anything. Do I need to remind you that the territory which we call Bosnia and Herzegovina today in the course of the twentieth century was made part of five -- as many as five states, different states. Do I have to remind you that in 1918 the Austro-Hungarian monarchy disappeared, that then the European political stage was entered by the idea of self-determination and with a big bang too, that at that time borders began to be drawn in conformity with the idea that the majority of people living in a territory have the right to decide in which country they will live and what that country will be called? In 1918 that principle was strictly complied with to the extent that in territories which were then -- this kind of distribution were in dispute, became the subject of a special referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not talking now about 1918. But let me direct your attention back to the 1990s. You appear quite prepared, sir -- I put this case to you: You appear quite prepared to make broad conclusions as to the Serb movement, the Serb plan, at pages 23 and 24 you say that the Serbian nationalist movement had clearly developed plans and a strategy of central secession, even a developed strategy of how to present its attempts in the media and hide its true aims and methods. Now, you seem to be quite prepared, sir, to state broad conclusions as to the Serb programme but you seem to be reluctant to draw conclusions about the Bosnian Croats, who were doing the same thing, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is far from -- they were far from being the same, because the plan that I talked about was the fruit of the action of a whole system of state institutions and non-governmental organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the Bosnian Croats did the same thing, didn't they? They established the HDZ party, which you described yesterday as the local branch of the Croatian part. They established something call Herceg-Bosna. They established the HVO. They established a government. They established a military. They established the police. They established a tax system and took control of most of Herzegovina during 1992 to 1994. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. They did not do the same thing, because in order for them to do the same, they would need to have an organised system which was already drawing -- which was drawing such plans as early as the 1980s. And you must know, and I believe you do, that the HDZ as a political party came into being in 1989 in a shed in Zagreb, that in Bosnia and Herzegovina the HDZ kept changing its presidents all the time, that this organisation was far from being a firmly -- a properly organised system, and that those two things are simply beyond comparison, and that all that I wrote and all that I said allows me to draw the conclusions which I do draw, and the conclusion that you draw, I cannot arrive at it nor can I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said, sir, in this regard, in your direct testimony, but you said -- and I think this is pretty much a quote "For a historian, the key thing is to be in constant contact with documents that pertain to the time that he is dealing with"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In preparing your report and stating the conclusions but you have, sir, did you examine or have the use of documents at the HVO archive in Zagreb? Did you consider those materials?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I have no access to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's a public archive, sir. Anyone can walk in off the street and access the documents, and many people, in fact, have done so. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I frequently visited that archive, but that archive keeps certain documents out of reach because there is a law which says that documents will be -- or rather, stocks made of these documents can be opened only after 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question stands, sir. Whatever limitations you want to put on and it what is there are not there. You have not used or considered any of the material at the HVO archives in preparing your report or reaching your conclusions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know how could I look at them if they were not accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you, sir, in doing your work interviewed any of the senior Croat and Bosnian Croat leaders or figures who were involved in the war during 1991 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally I did not, no. I did not interview anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've never spoken -- you've never spoken or heard from directly, as this Chamber has, for instance, Slobodan Praljak?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you ever talked to man named Ivic Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was his position in the Croatian government or in Croatian politics during the war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an adviser to the then-President of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Wasn't Mr. Pasalic in fact one of Franjo Tudjman's closest advisors?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know from the press, yes, and information that I had access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you ever interviewed or spoken -- obtained information directly from a man named Ivan Bender?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you ever interviewed any of the SDA or Muslim leaders in the Mostar region who were active in these events during 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you read or considered, sir, in reaching your conclusions materials from UNPROFOR, from the UN Protection Force, or from, for example, the British or Spanish peacekeeping units who were on the ground at the time? Have you considered any of that material?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those things that were published. But it is a very small number of documents, who, in one way or the other reached the press, be it Croatian or Bosnian or foreign.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you read any reports or materials from any other UN organisations or from the UN security council, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the decisions of the security council, some of the documents of some other United Nations agencies, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you read any reports or materials from the European Community Monitoring Mission, also known as the ECMM? Have you ever read those materials?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such material was never accessible to me. But in its view I read all that was accessible that was published as material, as reports of different government and non-governmental organisations, that is, everything that I had access to, just as I have read books of reminiscences of various participants in the events, journalists who covered the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I read books of reminiscences from -- by Richard Holbrooke -- from Richard Holbrooke to the general of the BH Army. I have read memoirs carried by newspapers, memoirs different peoples, again from generals to foot soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you read any transcripts coming from the offices of the President Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I had read the transcript which was published in Ciril Ribicic's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Have you read any other transcripts?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And yesterday I said -- sorry, may I be allowed to finish my sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I thought you were finished. Sorry. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ergo I read those texts which were published by the Croatian press and about which it is claimed that they are transcripts of the audio recordings done of various meetings held by Dr. Franjo Tudjman at the time when he was the President of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, how many such transcripts have you read, sir, the actual transcripts -- not the newspaper accounts but the actual transcripts in the Croatian language, how many have you read?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have absolutely no access to that material, my dear sir, because that material is inaccessible to anyone except those authorised by one of the state agencies of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir that, the government of Croatia has produced a number of those transcripts and provided them to the Judges in this case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. Now, how on Earth could I know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What's the problem? Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the problem is that I would also like to see -- I do not know that it was supplied by the Republic of Croatia -- by the government of Croatia. We heard different statements which were ad variance with what the Prosecutor is saying. And the government of the Republic of Croatia, Your Honours, has not provided a single transcript. This is not how we can behave in this courtroom that, the Prosecutor can say whatever occurs to him, especially when that is not true. We've had testimony when transcripts were tendered and we also had the testimony of the Prosecutor himself. And what the Prosecutor is now saying is not the same thing, but it happens to him very often. He always claims whatever suits him at any given time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- well, Mr. Krsnik, you have to understand the rules of the proceedings, you know. The Prosecution put a question to the witness. All we want to hear is the answer from this witness. We are not asking about your opinion, your views concerning this matter. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The witness has already said that he's not aware -- he was not aware of the fact that the transcripts have been provided, Mr. President. I would only make the shortest possible response. And perhaps counsel would like to, among other things, review the testimony of Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I can direct your attention to -- you've said that the HDZ was not -- to paraphrase, and I'm sure you'll correct me if I'm wrong. I think you've said a few moments ago that one of the reasons that the -- you wouldn't reach the same conclusion as to the HDZ as and HVO as you -- conclusions you reached concerning the Serbs is that they were not sufficiently organised. Now, you are familiar, are you not, sir, with the judgements in the Blaskic and Kordic cases? In fact, you've written about those judgements, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you to please look at Exhibit 946. Sir, have you reviewed -- does this refresh your memory about the conclusions that have been unanimously reached by six different Judges of this Tribunal about the fact that the conduct of the HVO, certainly in Central Bosnia, was a well-carried out planned campaign? And if you have something specific, I invite you -- if you have specific information to the contrary of these findings, please tell the Judges. Can you give us anything specific?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can. I can give you a very simple answer.
