With respect to what it says here, the persecution of the Bosniak population by Croat political and military authorities in the municipalities of Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak, gained momentum between January to April 1993, and in April 1993 resulted in a joint plan or idea, started and carried out by the leadership of Bosnian Croats to cleanse the Lasva Valley -- to ethnically cleanse the Lasva Valley of Muslims. Every year I travel through the Lasva Valley at least twice a year travelling from Zadar to Sarajevo, where my parents live today, and I can tell you that the Lasva Valley has not been ethically cleansed, neither of the Muslims nor of the Croats. If you can assure me that my eyes -- that my sight deceives me, that I do not see what I see when I go home travelling through an area called the Lasva Valley, then I will accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't ask --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But what I see with my own eyes remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you finished?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please continue. Then I'll ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The campaign of persecution of the Muslim population by Croat political and military authorities culminated in fierce military attacks on towns and villages in the municipalities of Busovaca, Vitez, and Kiseljak. All these localities which are the centres -- what in Bosnia-Herzegovina is called a municipality hardly deserved the name of towns. That is it. But I do not know what is meant by the fact that the Croatian forces attacked Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, yesterday you talked about Busovaca and you felt -- you felt quite knowledgeable about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while all due respect for your decision, I did not want to react until the witness answered, and always heeding -- heedful of -- mindful of the words of Her Honour Judge Clark and others. We really have excerpts from non-final judgements. These are not final judgements, and these are fragments of judgements that are not yet final. Do you really think it is proper to examine a historian about judgements which are not yet final, which have not been finally adopted by this Tribunal, and to use only fragments from them? But of course -- I mean, it is your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik -- Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I want to second the objections to this kind of examination. I cannot understand how can it be allowed to ask the witness to say a Chamber composed of six Judges established this or that. Do you agree with them or do you disagree? I think it is inadmissible. And then to be shown the witness fragments of judgements that he's not familiar with, that he is not shown, the things that have been established to be different, meanwhile not that mention how many differences there are between what the witness was asked and what is in the case truly. So my objection is that I cannot accept that the witness be asked the questions and that he is -- that he is invited to give his opinion about the decision of the Courts or that he testify against a Trial Chamber. I simply cannot accept that as an admissible question, and I am objecting to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I agree with Mr. Krsnik that those decisions have not reached the final stage, which means that in certain cases there's still appeal of the decisions made by the Chamber of the first instance. But the Prosecution invite this witness to make some comments about this judgement. In the legal -- you know, in the legal systems maybe the Trial Chamber have to be bound by the decisions made by the Appeal Chamber. But as a layman, as an outsider, especially as a historian, he has the right to comment on those judgements. I don't see there's any problem, you know, with this question. But it is time for a break, you know, Mr. Scott. Would you please save your question until we resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before the witness comes into the room, I would like to say that it is our intention to finish the testimony of this witness today, and I would like to ask Mr. Scott how long are you going to take for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll ask the Chamber to please accept my representation that during the break I slashed through, if you could see my outline, several pages of notes. I would very much prefer to finish today, but I think it would take me a full -- a full session, even with the edits -- even with the matters that you have cut, at the pace that we've gone today, I would say one session, this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So in this case, I would like to ask the opinions from both parties which we would sit in the afternoon. As far as I know, that we'll have the courtroom available this afternoon. Do you agree, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I absolutely agree, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Especially given the fact that I have deadlined, I have to travel to Mostar urgently in order to comply with all your requests, and that is another reason for which I am absolutely ready to work for as long as you tell us to stay here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the work in the afternoon is concerned, I agree, but I do not agree with the Prosecutor using the entire of today's session for several reasons: Firstly, his cross-examination is continuously longer than the direct examination. It would be justifiable if the cross-examination tackled relevant issues. Today we have been talking politics, which has opened this court through a very wide open door. I'm not here to talk about politics. I'm not here to defend my client's work from the Second World War onwards. We have the right here to deal with the indictment. We have the right here to deal with the things which are relevant for the indictment, and we shouldn't allow ourselves to turn this courtroom into a political platform. Our task from the beginning and our Defence has tried from the beginning not to address political issues. All the discussions that are being pursued here and all the questions, whether something has anything to do with the politics, we tried to reduce to the guilt of our client, whether he's guilty or not. But the way that Mr. Scott has cross-examined today means that we have opened the door to the politics, and that's why we have to go on working in the afternoon. I object to the Prosecutor being allowed to abuse our time in that way. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Par, to allow us to sit in the afternoon. I think we are talking about different matters. And as you know, that we are having a expert witness. In these situations, we will have the statement or report of that witness already. So I don't think you'll spend much more time on the direct examination. But in the cross-examination, there is a lot of questions that could arise during the report and during the direct examination. So generally speaking, the cross-examination should be a little bit longer than the Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 15842 to 15844. direct examination in the case of an expert witness. So we'll -- we'll sit in the afternoon. Could I turn to Mr. Naletilic. Mr. Naletilic, we are going to sit in the afternoon. Can you -- microphone, please. THE ACCUSED NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think that there will be any problems with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. So we decided that we will resume the afternoon session at 2.30 in the same courtroom, and we will finish this witness today. Madam Usher, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Mr. President, I would like to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we did not get translation. Would you please repeat again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please repeat. We didn't get the translation into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying that before the Prosecutor resumes, I would like an explanation to an answer that I didn't understand. The witness said as follows, that the culmination of the military campaign were attacks on Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak. After that I believe that the witness tried to deny the reality of those attacks. If we do not go back to that answer, I will not be able to understand all that. I didn't understand. I don't know whether it was something absurd that was said. Can you please explain before we proceed. Can you please shed some light on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I get the paper but you -- that I had in front of me before and from which I was reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think he's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were the excerpts from the indictment -- from the Court decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. It was probably put back together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was reading as follows: "Culminated in fierce military attacks on towns and villages in the following municipalities." The fact that towns are mentioned here reveals that it was written by somebody who doesn't know the situation in the area. And secondly, I, as a historian make a huge distinction between the term "attack" and the term "conflict." And if I may also add, it seems to me that here we come to a misunderstanding. As much as I respect this Honourable Court and its work, I still have something that one may call professional consciousness, and I don't think that the decisions of the Judges of this Tribunal imply the decisions for the history or the judgement passed on the history. I don't think that this Court testifies to the history or writes the history. And fortunately enough we do not live in a society in which the decisions of any Court are binding on the historians who will write history. That's what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not want to disturb either the examination or the cross-examination, but if somebody tells me that an attack is not the same thing as a conflict, then this confuses me even more. Maybe I am still asleep. But if an attack is not the consequence of a conflict, then I really cannot understand how the attack on Kiseljak, Busovaca, and Vitez can be a culminated point of the conflict. How can you say there is a difference between an attack and a conflict. I really do not understand and which maybe this gentleman who is a historian may help me so as to make my day really fruitful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The difference rises from the following: It arises from the way I make judgements and the way the Judges of this Court make judgements. The decisions of the Judges of this Court are influenced by the skills of the two sides that you have in front of you, and that is Defence on the one hand and the Prosecution on the other. And your decision will be influenced by the way they present things, i.e. the decision of the six Judges in question. My view of things is based on a different approach: I study what I find accessible in the way of documents, and based on that I create my own picture, my own judgement, and in my picture a conflict is generated from minute details, and it is a big question as to who in such a conflict is the side who launches an attack and who, on the other hand, is the side who defends itself. This depends on the point of view, on the materials that one uses in order to create his own picture, and certainly there must be a huge difference here between what I am saying, what is available to me, what I've used, and things that the Judges have used in order to arrive at their decision. Obviously there could be a debate on that, but it would require quite a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, do you mind if I say something to the witness? I don't believe but you appreciate fully, Professor Anicic, what the basis of a decision in the Trial Chamber s it is not based on the skill of the two sides in how they present things, but it is based on the evidence and the documents which are presented to the Court. If the Court arrived as a decision based uniquely on the skill of lawyers, the Judges could very easily be manipulated and blinded by skill. We have to make a decision exclusively on the evidence that's presented here, and that's why we have the system of cross-examining witnesses to see whether their evidence is credible. That's just by the way. The other thing they wanted to ask you just before the break, and I see that my colleague Judge Diarra has the same difficulties. Now, normally we would wait to the end, but as your evidence is very wide-ranging, sometimes asking a question at the very end brings us a way from the momentum of the dynamics of the evidence that you are giving. You stated that one of the criticisms but you made of the findings in Kordic and Blaskic is that they were based on an assessment or a verdict by the trial Judges that ethnic cleansing of Muslims had taken place in the Lasva Valley. And as I understand your evidence, you said but you travel regularly twice a year through that very area and that your eyes don't deceive you, but you see that ethnic cleansing has not taken place. What I wanted to ask you was: Do you mean by that that it wasn't totally successful or that it never happened or that there is an obvious sign of normal living activity in the Lasva Valley of people who were thought to have been expelled? I just wanted you to tell me on what basis do you make that finding. Did you stop and talk to people? Did you take lunch in an area that had a thriving Muslim community? Or is it just that you were driving through at 70 kilometres an hour and a few mosques were still standing? I'd just be interested in the basis of your assessment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The basis of my assessment is the fact that I stayed in the area for a while on several occasions. And to be very precise, you have to know that travelling at a speed of 70 kilometres an hour you can pass through it in about 15 minutes. So I spent some time there. I stopped there on several occasions. I had the opportunity to look at things more carefully, to talk to people living there. And given the fact that I've lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina for 30 years and that on numerous occasions before the war I travelled through that same area, I could conclude firstly that the successfully carried out ethnic cleansing, as it says here, did not take place and that the results but you can see today show that ethnic cleansing wasn't carried out. The second framework to the problem that appears here is the fact that the Lasva Valley exists in the broader context of the thing known as Central Bosnia, and the mere idea of the ethnic cleansing of the Lasva Valley is absurd in itself and sounds like a part of some grandiose plan because around the Lasva Valley there are a number of little hamlets or areas where conflicts never broke out and for which it doesn't say anywhere that they were ever ethically cleansed. And this is my general objection to what one can read in the decisions passed by this Court, or judgements passed by these Courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. And to follow up from that -- sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I can just say in your translation it says [In English] "It is absurd in itself --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That makes a lot of sense of what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Just following up from that so I can understand, because I don't want to interpose myself for counsel in this case. Are you saying that it is your view that there was no ethnic cleansing in the Lasva Valley, or that it was unsuccessful ethnic cleansing, or that parts were excluded? Because it's not clear from your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying is that there was no ethnic cleansing as the result of the existence of planned actions. If there had been something that one could consider ethnic cleansing, then it was the result of armed conflicts. And I believe that this should be emphasised very strongly. There is a big difference between the two things. On the one hand, that the conflicts were started with ethnic cleansing in view, on the one hand, and that the movements of the population were a result of the armed conflict, on the other hand. At least to my mind there is a big difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Professor Ancic, I'll try and digest what you're saying, but it seems to me that on the grounds, as far as the Muslim population or the Croat population is concerned, whether there's a grand plan or a spontaneous eruption of violence causing people to move, the effect on the ground is that the people are no longer there. But I won't enter into -- I'll wait and see what you have to say, and I'm sure it will be very interesting and Mr. Scott and Mr. Krsnik and Mr. Par can follow it through. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in reference to that - and my questions were similar actually to both Judge Diarra and Judge Clark before the break - if you look at the conclusions and findings, sir that, were reflected in Exhibit P946, what you have said, I put to you, sir, is that in terms of your coming back through the Lasva Valley and driving through on a couple of occasions, you may have the view that ethnic cleansing was not ultimately successful, but sir, the conclusions don't say -- I do not believe the judgements say, that ethnic cleansing ultimately was successful. The findings and conclusions are those respectfully, we submit, stated here, that there was indeed a plan, that there was a series of attacks, there was a series of persecutions against Bosnian Muslims in the area as found by the Judges in those two separate cases. Whether it ultimately succeeded or not was quite a separate matter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where did you --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please finish my thought. I'm waiting for the transcript to arrive at my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course. Please continue. We'll finish eventually.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The success criteria are used to measure the degree of organisation, and this is one of the things that needs to be taken fully into account when passing a judgement, and this is what I would like to add on to what you have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when were you -- you say you went there not only in response to Judge Clark's question, but you didn't just pass through driving rather quickly but you said you stayed in the areas. Can you tell me when you stayed and where you stayed and for how long.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spent the longest period of time in 1998, when, with a colleague of mine born in that area and who works in Zadar at present, I was going to a scientific meeting in Sarajevo, so we visited the place of his birth and we saw that the house he was born in was demolished in a village in the Lasva Valley in which there are no more Croats. That village is called Putkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who you think were you in Putkovici in this situation? How long were you there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And any other occasion that you've been in the Lasva Valley other than passing through?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I also stayed a while in Vitez in 1996, and that was the first time that I travelled from Zadar to Sarajevo, that is, it was possible to go there by car and one felt safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How long were you in Vitez on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of the fact that many displaced persons, probably from all sides - Muslims, Croats, Serbs - have returned to many of those areas, including Central Bosnia, since the war ended?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Many individuals did return, and it says likely as not that an equal number did not return. I've already quoted an example of the village of Putkovici, to which, for instance, the Croats did not return.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you really can't draw many conclusions from what you saw from one day in 1998 and three or four hours in 1996 about the conditions on the ground to the, or at least in 1996 and 1998, and what was the conditions on the ground in 1993 and 1994; can we? ?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot draw the conclusions as to what it looked like, but we can draw the conclusions as to how successful it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me take you and ask you- and I hope to move on -- and Mr. President, you'll notice that unfortunately since the break we've not made a whole lot of progress, I'm afraid. But to try to finish up on this topic before moving forward -- when you say -- I asked you a couple of questions before the break about the evidence that you have considered. Now in this case, but let me ask you similar questions concerning the Blaskic and Kordic cases, are you telling the Judges, sir that, you have reviewed the transcripts, the testimony of all the witnesses in those cases, all the Muslim who is came and testified, all the HVO documents that were put into evidence, all the ECMM reports that were put into evidence, all the British Battalion reports that were put into evidence, did you come to -- to disagree with the judgements arrived at by the six Judges of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I've told you that our ideas, our views, came about in a different way and on the basis of different kind of material, and I think that this is quite a clear answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in a similar way, sir, when the Judges in this case are asked -- will be asked, of course, to render a judgement, you have not reviewed all the evidence in this case either, have you, as we established, I think, this morning; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the interest of time, sir, I'm going to direct you only to two -- or three documents, instead of a considerable number more. But I could ask you please to find in your bundle P131.1. It should be in order. And if you will go down until you get to P131 with the assistance of the usher, please. I'll try to do these quite quickly if we can, sir. Exhibit 131.1 is a proposal by Jadran Topic, who was then the -- effectively the mayor -- the president of the HVO in Mostar, establishing another -- a number of municipal departments, general administration, finance, economic affairs, et cetera, et cetera. Could I ask you also -- I'll ask you the questions once in order to hopefully to move forward as quickly as possible. Could I ask you to also look at P164. It should be a number of exhibits down from that one, again, in order. Again, because of time I'm skipping over the exhibits in the middle.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. An interpreter's comment. The text -- the Exhibit P131 is a decision, not a proposal of a decision. The original say "Takes decision 2, establish."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My thanks to the booth for that. I was looking at the English, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, one of the things you've said today, and the reason I bring your attention to these particular documents among many others, is that the HDZ was not sufficiently organised to carry out any sort of plan of the nature that I've suggested to you. Do not these documents indicate in fact a high degree of organisation, a high degree of systems in place established by the HDZ and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. How -- what is it in this document that leads you to the conclusion that the level of organisation was high?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You don't consider that setting up the Department of General Administration, the Department of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs, Public Sector Affairs, public services -- sorry, my apologies to the translation. Department of Procurement, et cetera, the departments of the HVO, amendments to the decree on the armed forces, regulations on military discipline, creation of a central bank, you don't think any of those things reflect a high degree of organisation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, these are decisions establishing such things. If you cast your mind back, I spoke this morning about it, that the Serb side relied on fully integrated systems of state authority which needed no establishment or organisation, arrangement, and all these systems did not need to be translated into life, because they had been in existence before that for 40 years. And here we see that somebody is trying to organise something. I think that these documents set out to prove what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Could you please direct your attention to P175, which I hope will be the document following 164. If you'll look, sir -- if you cast your eyes over that document, in general terms, a report or minutes from a meeting on the 22nd of September, 1992. I believe the Chamber has seen it before. But is this not, sir, a veritable report, municipality by municipality by municipality, on the progress of the HVO in seizing power in each of these municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to answer to that that my methodology of work requires not to have a look at documents but to read them thoroughly, to know their source, whether they're authentic, what precedes them, and what follows in their wake. I cannot tell you what this document is unless I'm given some time to read it carefully and consider it carefully. So I'm sorry, I cannot give you that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, on -- in point of fact, sir, it goes back to the point we were making a few minutes ago. You've never seen these documents before, have you? In rendering any conclusions you've stated to this Chamber, you didn't have the benefit and are not considered any of in documentation, have you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Documents like this I did not have, because I said they were not accessible to me. I used documents which were accessible to me. And on that basis, I drew my conclusions and my ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you allow, sir, that in the case of both Blaskic and Kordic and in this case, this Trial Chamber, that the Judges of this Tribunal in fact may be substantially better informed on these documents and the evidence that's come before this Tribunal than you are? Not in your expertise. In the evidence that you've considered. Because you've told us today that you've never considered any of this. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: This expert is a historical expert, not a legal expert. This calls for a legal conclusion. It calls for speculation. I don't think it's a proper question for this expert, and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Meek, I think this question is a follow-up, you know, from the -- the question asked previously. But Mr. Scott, I really don't think, you know, the manner in this question is quite all right, you know. There's no comparisons, you know, between the Judges and this witness, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me rephrase the question. I didn't mean it in any event as a personal comment on either the witness or the Judges but on the evidence available and the information that's been considered in reaching both the judgements in this Tribunal and the conclusions stated and argued for by this witness. And my comment was, and if I could rephrase it:

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There's every indication, isn't there, sir, that the Judges of this Tribunal have had access to and have considered a wide range of evidence but you say you've never looked at; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that what you say is correct, because the Judges couldn't have had at their disposal the kind of knowledge which is the product of my life in Bosnia-Herzegovina and my study of the history of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the area for which I was hired. That is, what I am talk about is not -- what I am talking about is not the indictment as a whole. I am talking merely about the historical context of the war and how much history affected the way in which the war was waged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me recast my question, and I will move on, but I didn't -- my question again was not about your knowledge or expertise but about the materials, the source material, what we call evidence, that you've had available to you as opposed to the evidence that the Judges have had available to them. And you've agreed with me today, haven't you, sir, that everything you've seen, and the documents I've put in front of you, you've never talked to the witnesses. You've never looked at the presidential transcripts. You've never seen HVO documents at the archive that, you simply have not had access to the same -- you say, to the same evidence that the Chamber does. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have access to the same documents as the Chambers. That is true, and that is the only truth in what you just said. But I also want you, you and Their Honours, that the Judges neither had access to what I consider to be valuable proof of what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, sir. And presumably that's why you're here. We understand that. Now, let me go back to the ultimatum but you talked about yesterday, the political pressure that was brought to bear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Martinovic, what's the problem? THE ACCUSED MARTINOVIC: [Interpretation] One document. Let him produce a single document against Vinko Martinovic. He keeps talking about documents. Well, let him bring out one paper, just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, well, Mr. Martinovic, if you have some views and comments to make, my advice is that you go through your counsel. I believe but you are well represented by Mr. Seric and Mr. Par in this aspect. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My client's objection has to do with what I objected earlier, related to the manner of examination, that these things are not relevant to our defence. And we have been pointing out at it for a long time, so that I fully understand -- I fully sympathise with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I want to ask where does the debate for the -- which is one-hour long, this whole morning, where does it lead us? This debate about the examination, other cases, other Judges, different kind of evidence, a different area of Bosnia-Herzegovina which has nothing to do with our clients, except that Mr. Scott was also a Prosecutor in that case. And now with all these questions he obvious sets out to show him to be the champion of justice together with those -- justice. And if we follow the logic of those questions, we are again justice [As interpreted]. In the appeals procedure we have new documents which were not available at the time of the first Judges and these are of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the Judges and the Appeal Chamber they shed completely new light on the events that were referred to by these first instance judgements. And to be -- everybody in these Tribunal knows it. All of us who live and work here know that. Documents which were not available at the time of the first instance are available now so that a completely new light is shed and the question is what the judgements will be like, what is being done here, Your Honours, I think we're wasting too much time and -- with an inadequate witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, to answer the question put by Mr. Par, I would like to say this witness is an expert witness. His job is to make some comments on his report, which is not directly related to the counts charged in the indictment. As for the second question, raised by Mr. Krsnik, we believe that the Prosecution asked all those questions on that report, about his sources, about his authenticity, about what document the witness relied on. We believe those questions are allowed in this context. You may move on, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Going back to the question that I was putting -- in the process of putting to you, sir, before the interventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We talked yesterday about the ultimatum of the -- in April 1993, which you called political pressure by the HVO on the Muslim side. You are aware, are you not, as part of your historical research that the -- there was a statement prepared -- a so-called joint statement prepared by Mate Boban that Mr. Izetbegovic never signed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you're in a position to confirm to this Chamber, are you not, that in fact Mr. Izetbegovic never signed that joint statement, did he?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Just making a note. Sir, in the -- excuse me, Mr. President. I'm trying to move forward as quickly as possible. I just want to keep myself somewhat organised. Sir, do you recall -- I'm moving on and so the Chamber -- I'll be transparent. The final topic that I'll ask the witness about is so-called international armed conflict. Do you recall, sir, giving an interview in Slobodna Dalmacija about the Blaskic judgement? In fact, it takes us back to some of the topics that we talked about today. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to Exhibit 944, which I hope will be the next -- one of the next documents in the bundle that you have before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, while he's looking at that document, I will make a quick reference, because I am going to tender this document, based on what the witness just told us about the so-called joint statement. But because of time, I won't belabour it -- as Exhibit P273.1, which is in the bundle, which are the minutes of an HVO meeting on the 3rd of April, 1993. I'll come back to eventually. But I just wanted to put that in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your article, do you recall taking the position that in trying to explain the differences between the Blaskic sentence and the Kordic sentence was that Blaskic -- in the Blaskic case they found international armed conflict, and in the Kordic case they did not? Do you recall making that analysis in the article marked as Exhibit P944?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not an article. It is my interview. What is mine in this text is my answers. The layout of the text is the product of a journalist's work. So can we please confine ourselves to what are my answers. And if you tell me where that is, I would appreciate it no end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I do agree. And you're quite right. This is an interview format. Among other places, sir, I think if I can direct your attention to -- again, forgive me -- I can only refer you to the English text. But in the first paragraph of the section under "The type of conflict." And if this is not your words, then let me put it -- let me tell you what I'm referring to and then we'll clarify that. And if it's not your words you can tell me that. But it says that "One of the main reasons Blaskic was served a longer sentence compared to Kordic, despite a much more serious indictment of Kordic, is that the Blaskic judgement was reached by adopting the position of The Hague Prosecution, that the conflict between Bosniaks and Croats in BiH had been international armed conflict." Now, let's take it a step at a time. Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you -- is that --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement was that General Blaskic's sentence was decided only after an agreement was reached that it was an international armed conflict. My second answer was that I never saw the whole judgement pronounced on Mr. Dario Kordic, and that I do not know in how it happened that his sentence was much milder than General Blaskic's, and that I do not know to what extent has the thesis on the international conflict been embraced in that particular case, and that I do not know whether the duration of the punishment has to do something with it or not. The journalist interpreted my words freely in a way that he chose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, well, you've answered one of my questions about the interview but you gave, because I understood -- just so you know, and so it's transparent, I thought you had taken the position that an international armed conflict had been found in the Blaskic case but not the Kordic case, but that's not what you say. Correct? We've clarified that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware, sir, that international armed conflict was in fact found in both cases?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously I am not, because I've just told you that I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Then we can move forward, please, to the question of the involvement -- further involvement of Croatia in the conflict between the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that something that you have specifically studied, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I have studied this specifically in great detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me ask the question this way -- and perhaps we can see how far we get and we can shorten the rest of this. But do you -- is it your view that the Republic of Croatia was not involved in actively supporting the fighting on the -- excuse me, on the Croat side, in the Muslim-Croat war? Is that your view, or do you have no view on this topic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent to which the Republic of Croatia supported the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it also was to that extent involved in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is a number of the pieces of evidence published on that showing that from the very beginning the Republic of Croatia supported all those who stood up against Serb attacks in Bosnia and Herzegovina. If we follow that logic, then you can say that Croatia was indeed involved in this war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask -- if I can direct your attention, sir, to what's been marked as Exhibit PT8.1, which is -- as we represent, as I will explain to you, sir, is a transcript, what we've called a transcript from the presidential offices in Zagreb. This particular one, dated the 24th of April, 1993. When we talked yesterday, sir, about the fact of this ultimatum and you allowed that perhaps each of the three sides, even including the Serbs, but focussing particularly now on the Croats and the Muslims, had perhaps different views or visions of what the Vance-Owen Plan was about. And do you agree, sir, that in fact those visions also proved to be quite different?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were probably very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look, please -- and I'm going to direct your attention. And of course I know but you perhaps speak and operate in English quite well, so it's of course up to you which is easier for you, but I'll also give you the pages that I'm referring to in the Croatian language transcript. Initial Appearance going to direct first of all to the English version, which is on page 9 of the English transcript. And sir, you can either look there or I can tell you that in the Croatian language transcript, it is at page -- if you see the numbers that have been marked on these documents up in the upper-right corner, if you can find -- if you can find, please, 0132-2444. Maybe there's no -- no, there's no dash. But 01322444. I'll try to do this by only a couple of passages. Sir, this is a place where -- this is a meeting, just so -- this is a meeting in the offices of President Tudjman involving Mr. Tudjman, President Tudjman, Lord Owen, Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Boban, Mr. Petkovic and a number of people talk about the Vance-Owen Plan as it existed on the 24th of April, 1993. And the page that I've just referred you to, sir, Mr. Izetbegovic says at the top of that page, if you -- "Judging by the HVO actions, they understood this plan in a completely different manner, despite the fact that under the mediation of Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen we have signed a document, an agreement, whose first item explicitly say that is the provinces are not national territories of any one of these peoples who cannot claim it --" excuse me "who cannot lay claim to it only for themselves." The second item of our agreement say that "the symbols of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be respected and will also be displayed in the Travnik and Mostar provinces. In other words, Herceg-Bosna as a state entity, as a type of state entity could not exist after the signing of the Vance-Owen Plan." And I'll just use one other example and then I'll put a question to you. If you can look, please, at either page 11 of the English version, or if you've prefer to look at page 01322447. And again, it's Mr. Izetbegovic speaking. At about the middle of page 11 he says: "We have accepted the Mostar province but we have not accepted the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. We have accepted the Vance-Owen Plan because it envisages a province and does not envisage a Croatian Herceg-Bosna because Mostar is not and will never be only Croatian. You can terrorise Mostar for years, but you will never rule over it. So we can govern there jointly. Mostar cannot be governed only by the Croatian people." Now, sir, would that -- these passages, just as example that is I've given you, do you agree, then -- further agree that in fact despite the fact that there have been some signed documents at the end of March of 1993, there was in fact no agreement on the implementation of Vance-Owen, was there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would obviously like you to give me some time to read the entire transcript to be able to arrive at my own idea of this -- of what all this is all about. You have this habit of taking things out of the context. I don't have the habit and I would not wish to draw any conclusions based on what you choose as excerpts and what you choose to show me. So despite the fact what I already said about the alleged transcripts, because what you -- as you can see, there is no -- no sign of authentification to show that this is what you claim it is. In Republic of Croatia there is -- there are stamps which confirm the authenticity of any single document, unlike the Anglo-Saxon system in which it is the signature that gives the legal force to the document. In Croatia, it is the stamp that gives the legal force and authenticity to a document. For a document to be authentic, it should contain a stamp. Not even to mention the strange situation in which we don't know who was it who recorded it, who was it who wrote it down, whether the text was edited, whether somebody added something to it or omitted something from it. But despite all of these objections that I have, I would like to be able to read the entire transcript such as it is and then I could possibly tell you about the -- my impression of the atmosphere of that meeting, and I could then say how the authors of that meeting presented their views and what their views were. But now, for you to ask me to give you my views based on the five sentences taken out from a body of text, I cannot do that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can the witness be given the time to read the entire text. That would solve the problem. That is all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid not. The witness will spend another day here reading all the transcripts. There's volumes of documents. We'll see, you know, where Mr. Scott is leading us to, then we'll decide this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not a big document. It is 10 or so pages long document. It can be read quite quickly. We are coming to the break. And if all the time the -- we insist on the gentleman's comments, then maybe the gentleman should be allowed to read the entire document in order to be able to provide us with his comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It depends, you know, on the Prosecution, whether, you know, he would like to ask further questions and pursue that direction or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, that was -- the question I've last put to the witness was the only particular question that I was seeking to confirm with him further, and that is that even from the comments that I directed him to by President Izetbegovic, respectfully, I would submit, indicates a disagreement on the implementation of Vance-Owen. And that was the only thing I was trying to confirm with the witness. I have no objection if we're taking a break now if the witness wants to read the transcript that's provided to him, provided it's returned to the usher. I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, you are allowed to have that document during the lunchtime, and you can read it. And we'll continue with the cross-examination on the same subject after we resume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I have to remind you that we have received the documents and evidence on all these documents are received. So I don't think you are going to comment on authenticity of this document, and you may offer your interpretations on those -- on the contents of this document. We'll resume at 2.30 this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please address the Chamber. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, before the break we were on the Exhibit PT8.1, one of the transcripts, and you had indicated a desire to read the transcript in full. And so having done that, or at least I assume you've had the opportunity to do that. I'm happy to give you the opportunity to make any additional comments you wish to make about it, in terms of the question I put to you, that is, "Didn't it show, in fact a wide divergency of views on the Vance-Owen Plan?"

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what it shows. But you read the part of the text about which I still have some reservations, and you did the same like you did with my report and I believe you are authorised to do that. You've just taken out one part of that text. But I've read the entire text. That's what I asked you to do, and you only read one part, the words of Alija Izetbegovic accusing Croats for what they did. If this Honourable Chamber will allow me to do that, I would like to read three more short passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no objection, sir. And in fairness, let me say, sir, that I think that you've done me a number of times a disservice. The entire transcript will be in front of the Judges. They will have the entire transcript, not just the passages I directed your particular attention to. And I've given you this opportunity with the Judges' permission. And please do. Make the additional comments you wish to make.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to read three sentences said by Mr. Mate Boban during that same meeting, and I would like to read three sentences said by Lord Owen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, as the Prosecution said, that we have this document at our hands. We could read it by ourselves. If you have no further comments to make, let's pass this subject.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have this text and if you are going to read it, then I will limit myself to my comment only. It is clear from the text that I have in front of me that both sides have objections to the behaviour of the other side, and it is also clear that Lord Owen, who is the mediator, accepts that both sides make mistakes, and it is also clear that this is first and foremost a political disagreement, and that disagreement mostly is relative to the political future of Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e. it is relative to its constitutional and political order in the future. So that is what a transcript like that shows if it has been accepted as being reliable. What I find unacceptable is to take one part out of the entire context and represent that one part as an integral whole of its own as if there were no other parts of the same text. So that would be my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Sir, in connection with the historical work that you do, do you prefer generally speaking as a historian to base your findings on information from more than one source or more than one type of information?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most productive way to do things is to have different sources to rely on. Official documents, both those pertaining to the medieval times as well as those pertaining to contemporary times, very often provide a distorted picture of the reality in my experience. That is why it is very useful to have other types of documents available, because these documents will show how the official norms are applied in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of historical research, then, sir, you would find more confidence or have greater confidence in information or a point that you may be wishing to make if you had information from more than one source or information of more than one type of document; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In the bundle that you have there still, I hope, with you, down toward the end of that bundle now, can you please find Exhibit 664.2. If you look at that, sir, this appears to be an appointment or proposed appointment or a document listing appointments dated the 6th of November, 1993. And if you look at the last page of the Croatian language version, you will agree with me, won't you, sir, that at least on this particular version of this document there is no signature; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you see that the document nonetheless, sir, on the face of it, on the items 1 through 14, in terms of the appointments, is the -- concerns the appointments of essentially the senior officers of the HVO, starting with Ante Roso, going to Mr. Crnjac, and following; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, last of these transcripts that I'm going to direct your attention to, sir, is -- if you can find in your bundle PT 15 --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] It seems to be -- [Interpretation] This looks very mysterious, because on the first page this document starts with the appointment -- with appointments to the Croatian Defence Council, and later on I don't know what it refers to. Is that a document which was signed? Is that an official document? Does it have a stamp? Where does it originate from?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, hold that thought, sir.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And while we are still at it, some of the names here are familiar from newspapers. I know that brigadier Ivan Tolj discharged his duties and was in charge of political activities in the Croatian Army. That is why I find this confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if I start -- as I started doing a moment ago -- and if you'll keep that Exhibit 664.2 at hand, I'd like to direct your attention now to Exhibit PT15, another transcript which has been accepted -- admitted into evidence by the Chamber, dated the 23rd of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, in this instance, unlike what -- the way we've normally done it, I'm going to read a rather long passage for, I think, reasons that will become obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Before you do that, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Judge Liu and I can't find 664.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It should be -- Judge Clark, it should be there. But if it's not, we can put the English -- we can put an extra copy on the ELMO, certainly. Could I ask you to just put that on the ELMO, perhaps, if he wants to use the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's very difficult to find this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies for that. Again, the documents are not necessarily in numerical order in this instance but in the order in which we've used them in the examination. So the numbering may mislead you, and for that I apologise. If you have it --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct your attention to Exhibit PT15. And again, you can either look at the Croatian language transcript or the English language, whichever you prefer. If you look -- if you'd prefer to look at the -- if you'd prefer to look at the B/C/S -- or excuse me, Croatian version, I will say, you may look at page R0157079. And I am looking at page 7 of the English translation. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. By this record, this is President Tudjman speaking at this instance, and he's -- the part that says "president." "Mr. Minister and Mr. General, here with Gornji Vakuf we have experienced a political and military failure. Minister, you yourself know that today one of the joint chairmen asked in this context if we could and if we would, take control of Gornji Vakuf. And I gave you the task and it was not done, and in this way we have been militarily and politically compromised and we have given -- we have confirmed in this way the judgements that militarily we are not even up to the Muslims in this area. This is a fiasco. Who ordered the bridge in Mostar to be destroyed and why?" Then Gojko Susak -- it just says "rustling of paper. Nothing can be heard." President: "They've been showing it on European televisions for four days, and two days Croatian units shelling it. And accordingly please determine who ordered it and why and there will be dreadful political damage this has inflicted on us, that they be relieved and punished and see whether they can even be court-martialed. A written report about this, please." "Thirdly, how minister of Defence and chief of the main headquarters -- and the record will show that Janko Bobetko is here along with, Gojko Susak. How can you order confirming that Croatia is waging war, that it is directly involved? And I constantly emphasise but you should have built all this up as something voluntary that, these are volunteers who have left the Croatian army, who fight there under HVO command. And here you are appointing the main headquarters, Minister of Defence of Croatia, and the chief of the main headquarters. Susak: "Can I see that?" President: "You don't know that? Bobetko: "That is a proposal that I obtained for those people."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Stopping for the transcript, Mr. President, sometimes. Susak: "Who prepared this?" President: "You don't know?" Bobetko: "We here agreed that after the meeting here we should get together people who should help to work there." President: "But not that we should make appointments. It was said, if you please, that I released with my own order that stayed here General Roso. But General Roso was appointed by the president of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna." Bobetko: "Here are determined some men who will help -- selected who will help them? Help Roso in that group and that -- no one has, is --" President: "General Bobetko." Bobetko: "I propose men. I propose men in help them." President: -- Now, sir, when I direct your attention to your next portion I would like you to look at exhibit 664.2. "Look the Republic of Croatia, the Ministry of Defence Zagreb pursuant to our command of the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces Croatia, president of the republic, Tudjman, in accordance with Article 52 of the Defence law, Official Gazette number 74/93 and the decision on the foundations of the organisation of the Ministry of Defence. The following are appointed to the main headquarters of the Croatian Defence Council, or the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. First, Colonel -- Colonel General Ante Roso, the command of the main headquarters; Commander of the main headquarters of the Croatian Defence Council, that is, we, the Minister of Defence, signature of the Minister of Defence." Susak: "There is no signature." President: "And you don't know about that?" Susak: "I don't know about it." Bobetko: "This is our proposal about how we should form this group to help them. Help Roso. There is no headquarters at all, no command." President: "General, did you sign this?" Bobetko: "I looked at this last night, and I say now that these things have to be seen through to the end. This command has to be set up. It did not go anywhere. I don't know how it got here, but it did not go anywhere. We had to start from somewhere. Whom should we send there?" President: "We should have made an agreement and we should have sent people there." Bobetko: "Lucic got the assignment." President: "To send to Roso as commander of the main headquarters of the HVO who was appointed here -- there," excuse me, "who was appointed there by the main headquarters, not that we should appoint him --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Providing proof that we are giving the orders there." Susak: "These people are all there. Has anyone of them got there?" President: "What?" Susak: "How come I don't have that in my office?" Bobetko: "Whom? Who of them?" Susak: "Crnjac is there. Vrbanac is there, Biskic is there, Butorac is there." Bobetko: "Lucic informed them who was going down there. The assignment was to collect volunteers. Lucic got the assignment here of being responsible for the collection of volunteers." Now, I realise we've gone on for some time, but let me just look at one -- to shorten this -- well, I won't. I think it speaks -- the rest of the document certainly speaks for itself. Sir, would you agree with me as a historian that by all indications the document that President Tudjman; Janko Bobetko; and the Minister of Defence, Susak; were discussing on the 23rd of November, 1993, was the document marked as Exhibit 664.2?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am to agree with you, then I have to spend days and days pouring over this. Let me explain what is a trap in a historian's job. In the '70s of the last century in the former Yugoslavia there was a major debate among the historians about whether prior to World War II the then-political leader of the Croats, whose name was Vlatko Macek, communicated with the Italian Minister of Foreign Affairs or not, and whether that constituted an act of high treason. And the -- at the root of all this was a mysterious letter about a conversation with a mysterious Mr. Bombeles. There was even debate about it, doctoral thesis was written about it. And at long last the singular and agreed opinion was not arrived at, whether that particular letter was -- existed or did not exist as proof. And I'm mentioning just one problem. Here you are presenting very serious accusations, a very serious arguments. In order to accept them, one would have to go through the whole procedure of establishing the authenticity of such evidence, and that would necessitate special expertise. As a serious historian, that can be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just a final point on this. If I can ask you to look at page 10 of the English version or, if you want the use the Croatian version, of course you can. Simply by the description of the document given by President Tudjman, starting on the top of page 10, isn't that in fact the same text -- virtually the same text as on the beginning -- as at the beginning of Exhibit 664.2?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say in reply is that a description that one finds in one text corresponds to what is shown as another paper, that is, an indubitable fact. And I've said all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, a final question or two. In your interview that we were talking -- looking at earlier today. I think it's Exhibit 944. And again, I want to be sure that it's your words and not the interviewer's words, so that's why I'm going to be very specific to show you. Exhibit 944, sir. Can I again -- forgive me for referring specifically to the English text. But on the top part of the English page 3, it appears that the questions began wherever there is what I would call a dash or hyphen. For instance, at the top of that page there is a -- again, what I would call a dash or a hyphen. Then it says "To what degree can an appeal change the position of the Prosecution and the Court?" Now, do I understand that correctly, where -- that's the question of the interviewer that's being put to you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then as part of your answer, is it correct but you say,"The answer to such questions should be sought through the situation that has recently been created at The Hague Tribunal. Only Croats have been tried for Bosnian-Croat conflict so far." And this appears to be an interview given on the 11th of February of this year, sir. Are you aware of the fact that in fact in the Celebici case three Muslim accused were convicted by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they were sentenced for what?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't have the complete judgements, I admit to you, sir, before me, but I have the names. Mucic, Delic, Landzo, all convicted following a trial in this Tribunal. Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the names, but I do not know what they were convicted of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that there is an indictment pending in the Tribunal against Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was exactly what I said to the journalist. Obviously he made an error when transcribing the text from the tape, because this interview was conducted in the beginning of this year precisely at a time when the hearings in the case against General Halilovic, among other people, started. And that is what I referred to in my answer, in my answer to the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And there's also pending, is there not, at this time an indictment in this Tribunal against Enver Hadzihasanovic, Mehmed Alagic, and Amir Kubura; correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is exactly what I was talk about, because I read in the papers -- newspapers, excuse me, that there were indictments against them, that the trials had started, and that was why I said what I said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Your welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination? Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I shall try to be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I'd really like you to help this Chamber to finally complete this story about the historical context of a folk song. Can you please explain to the Chamber the following. My first question: Who were amongst the Ustasha ranks? I mean, people or ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ustasha included also a certain number of members of the then-Islamic faith, and I presume also those who belonged to the Muslim ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When did the Ustasha come into being?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ustasha came into being in the 20s of this century.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what was the historical context when the song "Jure and Boban" was created? Because it said that it is insulting to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- it came into being during the independent state of Croatia, something said -- to the Muslims. What does it? [As interpreted] I have to say one thing to the Chamber, and that is my experience, my experience in life, and that is that I heard this song in Sarajevo for the first time in 1992, in the early days of the war, and that the song was quite popular in Sarajevo in those early months of the war and its popularity derived presumably from the words "we shall ford the Drina and set fire to Serbia." However, when this song became offensive to somebody, that is a completely different problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Of course. But you as a historian, do you know why in Bosnia-Herzegovina, why are Jure and Boban celebrated in Bosnia-Herzegovina. What did they do for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, and I cannot say in Bosnia-Herzegovina they are celebrated, they are both celebrated and soon with different eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the fact remains that they largely conducted their operations in eastern parts of Bosnia, where in World War II -- where during World War II there was a conflict by and large between Muslims and Serbs, that it was within that context in a way -- in a form of collective image. At that time they had a completely different aura than the one they acquired after World War II.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I mean, what I'm trying to ask you as a historian, when they who saved the Muslims from Chetnik slaughters during the World War II in Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just said that they performed their operations in East Bosnia, by and large that it was there, where the war and combat operations were conducted against the then-Serb forces, which were called Chetnik forces, and that at that time in East Bosnia in point of fact there was no, just as there isn't any now, Croat population. So if they conducted operations, it remains that they were trying to protect the population of the area, that is, the Muslim population, from the terror of Chetnik units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And to conclude this story, if you would allow me to conclude briefly, did the Ustasha ever conduct any operation against Muslims? ?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Against Muslims alone, never, because after all there was an exclusively Muslim unit in the independent state of Croatia. It was called Handzar Division, Handzar Divisia, Handzar Regiment, and it was part of the German troops. It was called an SS regiment. So as an SS -- as a part of SS troops, it took part in the war on Germany's side, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'll also ask you a short and decisive question. So will you please try to tell us what is your view. Namely, when the Prosecutor examined you about conflicts and you explained it in your answer, what was your attitude, but the Prosecutor didn't tell you, and I will tell you, that the Prosecutor's Office claims that on the 16th of April, 1993, started the HVO attack on Muslim civilians and that that marked the beginning of the war. Not in Herzegovina alone. Across Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the text which I just read, as the transcript shows how erroneous is such a statement. It is a transcript -- the transcript of an audio recording of a meeting held in Zagreb attended also by Messrs. Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic, and they are discussing then numerous conflicts that had broken out by that time. So that is what I can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And so let us please go to the transcript but you have read as a whole, and I -- my question to you is: The Vance-Owen Plan, who signed it, who accepted it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was accepted by the delegations headed by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and the delegation headed by Mr. Mate Boban. Does this transcript say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This is implicit in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Now, I'm asking you that because the Prosecutor has been claiming for past year that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic never accepted it, let alone signed it. Now, either we have a transcript which is incorrect or something else is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just for the record, we have never taken the position that Izetbegovic didn't sign the Vance-Owen Plan on about the 26th of March, 1993. We have never taken the position. The joint statement dated the 2nd of April is a completely different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not correct either and I will prepare for my final brief. I am taking out all the interests parts of the transcript and will represent it, accurately with what the Prosecutor said in this courtroom and what he didn't and what the transcript says. So I won't go into it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Have you read Lord Owen's book?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And Richard Holbrooke's?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And in those books -- and I see it's implied by this text -- does in those books Mr. Lord Owen speaks about conflicts and attacks of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina against HVO units and the Croat population, equal in Herzegovina and in Sarajevo and across Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is mentioned in Lord Owen's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the detail where it is described how the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina went into hospitals and then fired grenades in order to provoke Serb reactions? Did they open fire in the corridors in Lord Owen's memories?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only Lord Owen's reminiscences. I watched this whole situation in a television/film. But you know, I'd rather not go into things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you familiar as the historian who was the first one to use the word "ethnic cleansing" and whether it was ever known before that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ethnic cleansing? I think it was used for the first time by an official of the American administration, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And was this term ever existed in history before that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That term was not used in this way. And if we applied it in the sense in which it is existed, this term could be, for instance, applied to the expulsion of 3 million Germans from Czechoslovakia. One could also describe a series of actions which took place in the world over during the past century, but that this term acquired its "popularity," in inverted commas, only thanks to the war in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I think this is my last question. In answer to the Prosecutor's question you were quite clear, but I'd like nevertheless to address you to some more detail. Of course it is possible. This term that we just mentioned, the intent to do it or because of conflicts, war, fighting, because where there is combat civilians have no place where there is combat, how would you comment on that, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, and that is my profound conviction, gained after all that I consulted prior to preparing my report, that there was the intent to set in motion large groups of people within a plan for the internal secession. On the other hand, I think that what at first glance really looks like ethnic cleansing, in the conflict between Croat and Muslim forces was the result of a military conflict due to divergent views as to the future of that country. I think that this would be a complete and integral answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm looking for a document that would show this -- the Prosecutor's attempt to show how well things were organised in Mostar. You already gave your answer, but my colleague is now looking for it, because something struck my eye, namely that on every page of this document of the Croatian version, because the Croatian is different, you know, one always has to examine both the Croatian original and the English translation. And on every sheet of paper, even though it is one document, but on every sheet of paper there is a reference number, and you as a historian of course -- let us finish because we're all tired -- to make a document a document and to make it acceptable to you, what are the minimum requirement that is it must meet and how does the document become authentic? Tell us was a historian. We as people, men of law know how it is done. But of course in our country, but perhaps in other systems there are different methods. But please tell us how you as a historian, what will you say tomorrow, historically speaking? Yes, this document is authentic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several criteria which allow us to judge the authenticity of a document.
