If a document has marks certifying it, which means its official authentification in a legal system, then such a document -- and if it has been preserved in its original form, then it is taken as an authentic document. Any type of irregularity in a document, if we are talking about official documents, makes it necessary to then check whether such a document is indeed authentic or not. The verification is always based on the requirement that this document must correspond to an identical document or a similar series of documents issued by the institution concerned. So that would be the basic criterion. However, as a historian, I must add something else, which probably looks different in my line of work than in the legal line of work. For a historian it is also important not only if a document is authentic from the point of view of the legal form. It is also important to know how well it reflects the reality. And that is what is very important in my line of work.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please switch on his microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the documents which were produced in the territory of, say, ex-Yugoslavia, say, military orders. When we are talk about life and death of people. Then political -- under -- by statute, if they are to be a document, mustn't there be a seal, stamp, and a handwritten authentic signature?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two elements of certification which confirm the authenticity of a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But I asked you because we do not have signatures in a number of document, even though in English it is translated "signed" even though they were not signed by hand of their authors.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In contrast with the Anglo-Saxon legal system, where a signature suffices to confirm the authenticity of a document. However, in the legal system or in the legal tradition which exists in this part of Europe, the stamp has the same weight if not more than a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: A signature which is -- which is handwritten or typed on a computer --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The signature must be by hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Anic, I have many questions for you which -- so I'll have to read your report again and again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In the context of the loyalties of the Croatian members of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the HDZ party and Dr. Tudjman, this is the context in which you have referred us to an incident which occurred when a tank unit was passing through Herzegovina on its way to Croatia. Now, that's the context in which I'm posing the question. We've heard about this incident from quite a lot of witnesses of very high standing in the HVO, and none of them has mentioned any role at all played by President Tudjman, and I'm curious about that, because if I read the document correctly and it's a translation, I accept, you have a reference, reference 70, to an author called Malcolm, and he says that he mentions this incident only in passing. But you go on to say that the author of this text, however, watched the whole event on a live TV broadcast. Are you referring to yourself, Professor Ancic?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Noel Malcom is the author of "Rare Histories of Bosnia." He didn't watch this incident, but he knew about that incident and he described it and I watched the footage of what was happening on my TV in Sarajevo. And I want -- what I wanted to say and point out was the moral authority that, at the time, Dr. Franjo Tudjman had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I accept totally the context and the reason why you referred to the incident, and that's why I prefaced my question by saying that. You -- as far as I can see, didn't intend to lay a huge amount of emphasis on the incident, but it was how the incident was brought to a close by somebody who had moral authority among the citizens of another country. I accept what you're saying there. But what I -- what I'm asking you about is your observation of the incident on Croatian -- sorry, on television in Sarajevo. Now, what I want to ask you is how did the people in the crowd know or become aware that President Tudjman was addressing them? What were the mechanics of that address to the excited group of people? We've actually seen some footage, I think -- well, maybe we saw a photograph. But we've actually heard a lot about this incident where a lot of people from -- I think it was the town of Siroki Brijeg -- surrounded the tanks and were there for several days and wouldn't allow them to pass, and we heard that President Izetbegovic with Mr. Stjepan Kljuic went down and addressed the people. And in fact, you've referred to that. But what we didn't hear about was the television broadcast. Could you elaborate a little on that, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This all aired on TV, so there is the footage but you saw, and President Tudjman addressed the people via the media, via the television and radio. So the official or the state radio and television network. So he was directly on air in the programme of the state radio and television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you know, I think I've led you astray when I said we saw footage. It was a different incident we saw footage of. We only heard evidence of this incident. But when you watched that on television in Sarajevo, it was long before the -- the referendum in relation to secession from Yugoslavia, from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I take it that tensions were not as high between the Croat and Muslim community at that time. I say this because we are aware that obviously when the war started, the various arms of the media tended to promote what they perceived was the truth and perceptions are what you deal with as a historian. Did you see that on a television programme which would be broadcast to Muslims as well as Croats? Would it have been a reputable television programme?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment I cannot remember which of the channels of the state TV was that on. In Sarajevo there were three channels of the state television, and there was also a special channel which showed the programmes edited by a group of journalists from all over the former Yugoslavia, and that channel or programme was called Yutel. Now, which of these channels broadcast that particular thing, I can't remember. But at the time those were the only TV channels, not only in Sarajevo but in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Did you have any reason not to believe what you saw on television, or did you find any confirmation for the truth of what you saw on television by reports in any other form of media the following day, or from talking to your colleagues, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events received comments in the other media, and television itself is not a media that shows only the truth and nothing but the truth. It can easily be manipulated. But I didn't find any reason to doubt what I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions? Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One, if I may, and that is the question -- I don't know whether my translation is good. I was look at the question posed by Her Honour Clark who said that Mr. Tudjman had influence on the citizens of other states. I'm talk about the convoy, if I understood the question well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, the citizens -- the Croat citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were members of the HDZ, in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we then talk about the citizens of another state?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those were citizens of same state, because this happened even before the formal break-up of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You're right about that, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to give your evidence. Madam Usher will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage any documents to tender? Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we would have only one, D1/316.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any objections, Mr. Scott? That is the report of that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No objection to the admission, obviously subject to all the questions, cross-examination, et cetera. But no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course. This document is admitted into the evidence. And on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was just going back through the list. I'll try to do my best now. I will double-check myself, if the Court will allow. And if I mind I make an error, I'll try to correct it. But based upon the documents that were actually used with the witness today that were not already admitted, Exhibit 131.1, 273.1, 830.2, 941, 943, 944, 945, 946, PT8.1, and I guess we'll need -- it doesn't matter to me, really, but you can either admit the transcript of the "Jure and Boban" song which was previously tendered by the Defence, D1/277, or it can be given a Prosecution number, whichever the registrar prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. And I would kindly ask you to give us some time to comment on the new documents, because we have to check which ones the Prosecutor used today, which ones he didn't use, and I would like to comment upon these documents. Secondly, Your Honour, another request that we have: We are asking from the colleagues from the Prosecution that all the documents for which the designated source is the BH government or the BH embassy, can they please tell us who provided them with these documents, because here they mention an organ that doesn't exist. And for every document we've heard the testimony of the professor today, every document has to contain a signature or the minister or the deputy minister in order to be valid, and we have to check -- we have to see whether all these documents do indeed bear such signatures and co-signatures. And this will also apply to all the other documentation for which the indicated source is the BH government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I've forgotten something. If I may, my colleague has just given me a document we would like to tender, a Prosecution document, P5960. Can this be admitted into evidence because it has been used in the examination, obviously subject to the Prosecution's approval, P960. I'm sorry. I apologise. The number was wrong. P960.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We do object. The only reason it was brought up was it was marked for purposes of the showing -- asking the witness questions about it. It did not go into the substance of the document at all, and it's irrelevant, and it was only marked for the purposes of asking the witness if he had in fact contributed to it, so yes, we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we also believe that document is irrelevant in the content of that document. We decided that -- not to admit that document, that is, document P960. I could give you some time on your comments of all those documents tendered by the Prosecution, but you have to know that this is the last witness in the Defence case. We would like to have a sort of clean slate before the rebuttal and the re-joint procedures. So I hope you would file your objections concerning this document this week so that the Trial Chamber could act sometime next week. As for the third matter, this Trial Chamber has no doubts about BH government and the BH embassy at all. I think it's not possible for the Prosecution to provide you who in that government in the embassy provided those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in that case I have a feeling there may have been a misunderstanding. Are you telling -- are you saying that I'm not telling the truth? Because we have proven that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina doesn't exist, and the Prosecution cannot indicate a non-existing organ as the source of their documents. There's something wrong here. That organ does not exist. That's why we are asking for that. And you will be able to see for yourself that there is just one segment in Bosnia and Herzegovina that could have provided them with the documents, and those are Bosniaks, i.e. their representatives, and that is AID. Another thing, Your Honour, that I would like to ask you: In one of your decisions you stated that all the documents that have been provided by the United Nations are indisputable, so far I haven't objected to any of them, the Washington Agreement, The Dayton Accord, and all the other documents. I can tender them for admission before the rebuttal, because they cannot be objected to by any of the sides. That's your previous decision when it comes to the documents issued and provided for by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think you know, you somehow misunderstand what I mean concerning with the UN documents, you know. I think the rule is like this: All the documents tendered, unless otherwise stipulated in other articles or Rules of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence have to go through a witness. This is the practice from the very beginning to the end. We introduced those documents through a witness. There should be no doubt about the authenticity, about the source of those documents. The only criteria is the relevance of these documents to this very case. You could not introduce, you know, hundreds of the UN document to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not, Your Honour, but I believe that the Vance-Owen Plan, the Washington Agreement, and the Dayton Accords must be integral parts of this file, because the Dayton is the beginning of today's Bosnia, the Bosnia that came by -- into being in 1995 and still lives. And if that is the case, then I will formally use my witnesses in the rejoinder, and through the witnesses I will tender these documents for admission because I believe -- the Defence team here believes that these three documents have to make an integral part of this file, of this case, and we are going to provide you with a motion so as to not waste your precious time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think my lead counsel wishes to ask that before we end our case, which we haven't quite, because of the rejoinder and rebuttal, that the Court -- the Trial Chamber take judicial notice of these three documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. That's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You could file your motion concerning with the Rule 94, that is the judicial notice, and explain your reason for submitting of those documents. I think this Trial Chamber will consider your motion in accordance with the Rule 94 in this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, that's -- Your Honour, judicial notice is -- these documents are easily accessible, they're widely known, and we'd ask you orally now to take notice of the judicial notice of the documents. I don't believe the Prosecutor will have any objection to that procedure, those three agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, forgive me, Mr. President. Mr. Stringer and I were just discussing. I think it's our -- please allow me to correct ourselves on further review, but it's our position, I believe, that the Vance-Owen Plan is already in evidence. It was signed, as I said earlier today, I think the 26th -- well, signed by the Croat and Muslim sides. It was never signed by the Serbs, of course. But it was signed the 26th of March, 1993, and again no matter how many times Mr. Krsnik says to the contrary, it's never been our position that Mr. Izetbegovic didn't sign it on the 26th of March. I think the Washington Agreement is also in evidence, I believe. I think of the three the only one that might not be in evidence would be Dayton. We would look at that, Mr. President. I suppose it -- surely a true copy of the Dayton Agreement can be found. Off the top of my head I'd say I'm not sure of the relevance of it frankly, because it was not in the late 1995, well after all at the events in this case. But we can certainly look at the -- look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this Trial Chamber has to do some research on this aspect too. We see whether these three documents have been admitted into the evidence or not. If not, if not, we will make the proper decisions concerning of whether we are going to admit them or not. The last matter: Yesterday was the 23rd of September. That is the last day for the Defence counsel to submit their motions for the rejoinder witnesses. Up to now we haven't received those motions yet. I just want to check it. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we gave it yesterday to the Registry to our good and worthy Laurent, as we call him. So maybe it hasn't reached you yet, because we started early this morning. And in that motion we have expressed all of our concerns, and what we have written, we -- I'm going to briefly inform you about. We have mentioned some of the witnesses, but for the -- due to the brevity of time between Friday and Monday, I couldn't do everything. We have just indicated the names of the people that we expect, and I am going to confirm that from Mostar to -- and inform my team, because I'm travelling to Mostar tomorrow. So we have indicated four possible names, so to say, out of whom one is -- has been confirmed. And for the others, I don't know, Your Honours. It may happen that some of them will not be able to come. I just have to verify. And I can't be in two places at the same time. I have to go there. And by Friday the latest you're going to get the second and the third name, possibly if you allow us to proceed in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But -- but I hope that motion will not only mention the names but also the substantive matter that you are going to use in your rejoinder so that the Prosecution can make a timely response to your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, exactly. My questions are going to be the answer to rebuttal, the purpose of the rejoinder is to answer to the rebuttal, and we have indicated the questions that we will be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, our Defence has already filed a submission and we have received the confirmation from the Registry that it has been received, so I believe but you will have it in the course of the day today. So in brief what we have asked in our submission, with regard to the fact that one witness has been called to -- has identified here the so-called wooden rifle. We have asked from the Chamber to issue an order to the Prosecution to provide us, to give us that wooden rifle if it exists, to tell us where the wooden rifle comes from, what is -- what are its origins, and in case we receive all that, we ask for the approval to have the wooden rifle assessed by the experts of the institute for criminal expertise in Zagreb. So this is what our submission contains in brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I would -- I was just informed about -- by Madam Registrar from D1/277 is marked as P961, document P961. Well, I think we are adjourned until the 7th of October for the rebuttal and the rejoinder procedures. We will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 3.58 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 7th day of October, 2002, at 9.30 a.m.
